text.p: The number of Britons who say sleaze allegations could influence the way they vote in the British election is astonishing, a leading pollster said on Monday in reaction to a Reuters opinion poll conducted by NOP.
Robert Worcester, chairman of polling organisation MORI, said the May 1 ballot could be decided by people who have not yet made up their minds.
"If as many as six percent of the electorate were to be affected by the sleaze issue it would mean the votes of nearly two million people changing sides," he said.

The poll of 1,088 voters across Britain published on Monday asked how much the recent allegations affecting the ruling Conservatives might influence the way they intended to vote. Six percent replied "a lot".
"Nearly eight in 10 voters said it (sleaze) wouldn't affect their vote -- that's to be expected. That as many as six percent said that it would "a lot" is astonishing," Worcester said.
"Three hundred votes in a constituency isn't a lot, but if as many as 300 Tory (Conservative) voters in 1992 had switched sides it would have reduced John Major's majority by half," Worcester said.
But he doubted this poll finding would translate into an equivalent outcome at the election, which all polls suggest will result in the Conservatives losing power.
The poll put opposition Labour 21 points ahead of the Conservatives, with 51 percent support among those expressing a party preference. The Liberal Democrats took 11 percent.
The Conservatives' election campaign has been marred by a string of allegations, including the so-called "cash-for-questions" saga and a series of sex scandals.
